newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia diesel glut spurs near-term concerns.
newsitem.headline: Asia diesel glut spurs near-term concerns.

text.p: A flood of diesel oil into Asia has raised concern over the region's ability to absorb the glut but in imports will still be required in the longer term to meet bourgeoning demand, analysts and traders said on Thursday.

Since March, more than 15 million barrels have been shipped to East Asia and India from Europe, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, Russia and the U.S., spurred by a buying frenzy by independent Singapore traders who bought more than 14 million barrels.
This is the largest ever flow to Asia and is piled on top of the region's 5.1 million barrels per day (bpd) diesel output.

The purchases by Hin Leong Trading, its sister company Sanko Oil, and Japanese trader Marubeni International Petroleum Co, helped support prices despite soft demand from China and Indonesia, the region's major buyers.
"What is critical to look at is that because of the artificial price level, the region is attracting so many barrels," a European refiner said.
He said one concern is that Western refineries, encouraged by the purchases in Asia, are "pumping up" production at a time when they normally cut output amid low demand.
But analysts said while Asian refiners have raised crude refining capacity, the result is a surplus in gasoline rather than diesel, which would be in deficit until 2000.
Sara Banafzak, a researcher with Honolulu-based think tank East-West Centre, said Asian diesel demand now outstrips supply by about 600,000 bpd.

She estimated Asia's 1997 imports from within and outside the region at 1.16 million bpd, with India taking 413,000 bpd and China 128,000 bpd. By 2000, Asia's diesel demand would hit 6.6 million bpd, with output at 5.6 million bpd, raising imports to 1.5 million bpd.

Banafzak said despite a dramatic rise in South Korea's refining capacity to 2.2 million bpd last year which enabled the country to hike exports momentarily, growing domestic demand would eventually cut exports.
Asia would also be short of low sulphur diesel in the next two years as Japan, South Korea, Thailand switch to the 0.25 and 0.05 percent grade, followed by Taiwan in 1999.

Despite the optimistic long term scenario, analysts said major buyers such as China are unpredictable. After buying about one million barrels in December, China decided to curb first quarter imports and raised domestic output.
Traders noted the volatility of Asia's spot market which made large imports from the West destabilising to the region's near term demand-supply balance.

"What will happen to the surplus barrels that have flooded this region, where will they go to ?" the refiner said. "These barrels will stay for a long time before the market reaches equilibrium again as regional demand is now very finite."

A Western trader said it was not healthy when the market was at the mercy of one or two buyers. Traders fear prices could collapse if the buyers suddenly withdrew, while there is insufficient tank space in Singapore to store the cargoes.

Traders are also apprehensive because of lack of transparency in the movement of these cargoes as the bulk are shipped though a fleet of 90 tankers owned by sister company Ocean Tankers which also act as floating storages.

Latest data from Singapore's Trade Development Board showed a build in middle-distillates stocks of 452,000 barrels to 7.04 million barrels, the third week inventory has risen. Amid the glut, prices fell below $27 a barrel on a free-on-board (fob) basis this week, from more than $28 at the peak of the buying spree.
But a Singapore refiner said the concerns maybe misplaced as buyers were confident of selling their cargoes to endusers and have lifted half their total purchases.

He said Hin Leong raised spot purchases in Singapore as it has stopped buying Middle Eastern and Korean term cargoes. It used to buy four diesel cargoes from Korea and two million barrels from the Middle East per month.
